extracted.intended_audience: students of Stoicism and general readers seeking to compose a personal handbook of Stoicism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and practicing from a self-authored handbook of Stoicism: daily exercises, conceptual knowledge (passions, virtues, vices), practical routines (journaling, gratitude, time management), and remedies for passions like anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of conscience / daily self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: When entering their homes, inquire about the errors committed during the day and on which occasions you would have acted differently; review each daily action: 'What was done wrong, what was accomplished, what remains for you to do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice nightly review (Epictetus, Pythagorean/Socratic precedents). Examine everything from first to last act, take responsibility for wrongs, rejoice for what was done rightly. Can be done in solitude; the exercise refines critical thinking and is the foremost task for the student of philosophy. Seneca's nightly routine: meditate after others sleep, consider where you fell short and plan improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have the Tenets at hand (memorize & internalize maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The student must have at hand—the tip of the tongue—the main maxims of Stoicism to carry out proper self-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undertake reading of ancient texts, underline important passages, jot margin notes, then transcribe underlined parts into a notebook or journal and paraphrase them in your own words. Gradually revisit and paraphrase notes to internalize reflections and build a new inner discourse. The aim is embodiment of theoremata, not erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to embody principles, not to display erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective of study is to embody the philosophical principles (theoremata) and progress toward virtuous action, not to become erudite or boastful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use texts and exercises to produce an inner discourse aligned with reality; practice privately rather than for show. Epictetus notes Socrates questioned and examined himself when no interlocutor was available; avoid showing off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid showing off; maintain humility about wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume or proclaim you are wise; wisdom is recognizing how little human wisdom is compared to divine wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates' model: wise insofar as one recognizes one's own ignorance. Treat wisdom as an ongoing, imperfect project — progress, not finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-communion and self-forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Your philosophical diary should include self-consolations to neutralize suffering from external losses and personal mistakes; forgive yourself and start over many times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use journaling/soliloquy to establish dialogue with oneself, temper expectations, and allow repeated recovery from stumbles. Remember human fallibility; the practice is part of self-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise gratitude (eucharistia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly remember the gifts of fortune and those who helped you—teachers, family, tutors, gods—and acknowledge both great and small blessings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List those who aided you (Marcus Aurelius model), jot down gifts when possible, and practice gratitude for small daily things (warm bread, breeze, sunrise) to prevent resentment and cultivate happiness. Plutarch and Antipater of Tarsus provide corroborating examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision of wholeness / 'vision from above' (experience the Divine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the things of the world as a whole and insert yourself as a participatory part of the Divine Intelligence — 'vision of totality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek open, extensive places (deserted beaches, mountain viewpoints, waterfalls, caves) to perceive physical smallness and experience connection with the Cosmos; reflect on the experience in writing. If mobility is limited, lie on the ground and look at the starry sky. Use the experience together with gratitude to purify the heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand passions as epistemic movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are movements in the soul tied to judgments/assents: some correspond to correct beliefs (good emotions) and others to false beliefs (bad emotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the natural state is tranquility (ataraxia); bad emotions are asymmetric, irrational movements arising from assent to false representations. Training targets the epistemic origin of passions (assent) so one can remove false judgements and thereby remove corresponding passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of evil passions (four main genres)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoic taxonomy: suffering (lype), fear (phobos), appetite (epithymia), and pleasure (hedone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn these four basic passions and their subspecies so you can identify your emotions, perceive epistemic flaws, and work to eliminate bad passions while cultivating good ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of suffering (types of lype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion (eleos), envy (phthonos), jealousy (zelos), rivalry (zelotypia), weight (achthos), affliction (ania), anguish (odyne), inattention (synchysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the definitions and recognize these variants in yourself; understand Stoic prescription to be in solidarity/help rather than suffer with those who appear to suffer unjustly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of fear (types of phobos)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify anticipations of evil resulting from false assent; distinguish species to better target training (e.g., shame vs tremor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of appetite (irrational desire / epithymia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack (spanis), resentment (thymos), rage (orge), passionate love (eros), wrath (menis), hatred (misos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize irrational desire as assent that something nearby is a good when it is not; mapping species helps diagnose and correct desires via reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of false pleasure (hedone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malicious joy (epikairekakia), perverse delight (terpsis), wicked rapture (diachysis), enchantment (kelesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pleasures result from assenting that a present good is truly good when it is not; awareness prevents dissolution of virtue by deceptive pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vices as ignorance; four main genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices (each a kind of ignorance) are: imprudence (aphrosyne), intemperance (akolasia), injustice (adikia), cowardice (deilia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that bad passions stem from these ignorance-types; moral education aims to replace each ignorance with its corresponding wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom as remedy; four corresponding virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedy to vices is wisdom (sophia) divided into: prudence (phronesis), temperance (sophrosyne), justice (dikaiosyne), courage (andreia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate these virtues as knowledge of what is good/bad/indifferent, what to seek/avoid, what is due to others, and what to fear or not; developing these yields good passions and virtuous action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good passions and their types
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic good passions: rational desire (boulesis), care (eulabeia), contentment (chara) with species such as goodwill, benevolence, shame/dignity, delight, convivial joy, contentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake Stoicism for suppression of all feeling; aim for development of good passions grounded in knowledge, which produce harmonious movements and virtuous feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies against anger (Seneca's strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical medicines to guard against anger: (1) give time to time (count to three), (2) suspend judgment about others' intentions, (3) avoid getting angry over small/insignificant things, (4) remember your own vulnerability (clause of reservation), (5) reflect on the imperfect nature of humanity and respond benevolently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger is assent to the need for revenge; halt progression from bodily impulse to assent. Use staged responses (pause, withhold judgment, expect human faults) and education from childhood. Aim to observe humanity benevolently and attempt to dispel ignorance rather than vent fury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect on and fulfill social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditate on the roles you play (good father/mother, son/daughter, neighbor, citizen, spouse) because virtue and happiness depend on fulfilling these roles correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism emphasizes practical duties over grandiloquence; reflect on what is fundamental to human life and the duties those roles entail, especially in a society preoccupied with pleasure and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time wisely; meditate on ephemerality and manage time
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly reflect on life's brevity and manage the time given: 'Live immediately!' Seneca's summary: life is short only if time is not well employed; many seek leisure but don't attain it; idleness often means indulgence in empty pursuits; true leisure is philosophic study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: (a) list places where you spend time during the week; (b) reflect where time is wasted or not beneficial to spiritual/mental health; (c) reorganize time, reserve portions weekly for philosophy reading/reflection and for physical exercise (walks, bike rides); (d) eliminate/minimize conversations and places that add nothing positive. Use Epictetus' exercise of naming the nature of things (e.g., 'I like a clay pot') to loosen attachment and reduce disturbance.
